pull_request.title: Calorimeter: default Si-W ECAL to reusable wedge mothers
pull_request.head: codex/siw-ecal-real-wedges
pull_request.body:
## Summary

- Default LAYOUT-001 to reusable real Si–W wedge mothers for the barrel and both endcaps.
- Preserve the stock replica metadata, readouts, physical leaf geometry and material definitions. The standalone export and earlier compacts retain the legacy assembly path.
- Refs #117 and #118, DES-030 and DES-031.

## Validation

- Fresh default export, factory builds and all 38 calorimeter hardware and composition tests passed.
- All 531,936 Geant4 sensor placements and native DD4hep lookups agree with stock IDs and transforms. All 65 tracker-plus-ECAL material rays agree.
- The full tracker-plus-ECAL ROOT scan found zero overlaps or extrusions at 10 nm. Three fixed-transverse-momentum electron smoke events passed persisted truth and hit-ID checks.
- The ECAL-only DDG4 map build took 23.0 s. The retained stock measurement on the same node took 65.9 min.

The validation report includes the measured scope and reproduction commands. Shower-response equivalence requires a dedicated study.

## Merge preparation and accounting

Human review by `asalzburger-review` approved `9f2e135ca4c31264248efe2250334d76d2b741cd`; no unresolved inline threads. The PR is ready for review. The closing commits update records only; their hosted checks are verified separately.

Exact client observations across 12 completed turns (290 requests, including SysArch and PhysVal): **76,100,346 input + 173,977 output = 76,274,323 total tokens**. Cached input 74,506,496 and reasoning output 62,803 are subsets. Six canonical work labels cover sample/compute pilot, startup profiling, barrel prototype, endcap prototype, default implementation, and merge preparation. The current active publication turn, other devices and automated-review history remain outside this observed subtotal; execution models are unexposed.

The user explicitly approved publication of the prepared token and interaction records. The paired merge-readiness journal and the two PR129 inventories under `logs/usage/` retain exact completed-turn ownership, dates and recovery provenance. The per-PR interaction ledger includes the refreshed public review and 12 curated visible-turn snapshots. Shower-response equivalence and the angular resolution study remain follow-up work.

events.text:
The EM calorimeter is in a baseline state now:

- next we would like to see for a reference E_T = 50 GeV the sigma(E)/E versus phi and eta
- ideally with magnetic field = 0 and no inner tracker 
- best with electrons



What would be a reasonable sample given that eta can beseen at |eta| and phi also has a foldable symmetry ?
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: I’ll check the baseline geometry and simulation setup to see which symmetries the scan can use and how many electrons it needs.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text:
For the nODD **Si–W ECAL baseline**, I’d budget **about 110,000 single-electron events**. Use 96,000 for the main map and the rest for symmetry checks and targeted points near cracks and the barrel–endcap transition.

- **Gun and geometry.** Generate one \(e^-\) per event from the interaction point at \(p_T=50\) GeV, with \(B=0\). Keep the barrel, both endcaps and their local passive material. For this ECAL-only reference, I’d omit the inner tracker and beam pipe. At fixed \(E_T\), the electron energy is \(E\simeq 50\cosh\eta\) GeV, so it reaches **188 GeV at \(|\eta|=2\)**, **503 GeV at 3**, and **1.37 TeV at 4**. I’d take the first map to \(|\eta|=3\).
- **Main grid.** Use **16 \(\eta\) points × 12 local \(\phi\) points × 500 electrons**. Sample the full signed \(22.5^\circ\) sector and put six of the \(\eta\) points between 1.30 and 1.60 to resolve the transition. Add explicit points at the sector centre and on both sides of a seam, since the coarse grid can miss narrow cracks. With 500 events, the statistical error on a near-Gaussian width is about **3.2% relative** per point. [Barrel geometry checks]([redacted] · [NIST width uncertainty]([external URL redacted; see source journal])
- **Folding.** Fold \(\phi\) modulo \(22.5^\circ\), keeping the sign of the offset from the sector centre. For the two endcaps, the placement rotation pairs \((+\eta,\phi)\) with \((-\eta,-\phi)\) modulo the sector period. Check matched directions before pooling in \(|\eta|\), especially in the barrel and transition. The barrel’s staggered layers already give **38 versus 36** active-layer crossings in the geometry model at \(\eta=\pm1,\ \phi=0.03\) rad. Keep signed results wherever the response differs. [Barrel ray model]([redacted] · [Endcap placement]([redacted]

For each direction, plot the **mean response** and **\(\sigma(E_{\rm reco})/\langle E_{\rm reco}\rangle\)** together, and record the zero-response fraction. At a seam, the width can be undefined when the signal vanishes. The existing Si–W endcap study saw exactly that at its seam point with 50 GeV beam energy. [Endcap seam study]([redacted]
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: Can you run a test sim of 100 events and estimate the necessary compute ?
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: I’ll use the acts-spack skill to verify the Geant4 runtime, then time a 100-electron pilot with the Si–W ECAL, zero field and the tracker removed. I’ll measure startup and event processing separately so the scan estimate accounts for job size.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text:
The **100-electron Geant4 pilot completed and all 100 saved events passed validation**. For the proposed **110,000-event Si–W scan through \(|\eta|=3\)**, I’d budget **about 77 core-hours, 20 hours wall time with four workers, and 500 GB of scratch space**. The raw EDM4hep output projects to 464 GB, compared with 154 GiB currently free on the Mac Studio.

| \(\eta\) | Beam energy | Measured time per electron |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.50 | 56.4 GeV | 1.01 s |
| 1.45 | 112.4 GeV | 1.71 s |
| 2.00 | 188.1 GeV | 3.33 s |
| 3.00 | 503.4 GeV | 8.26 s |

The pilot took **78.9 minutes**, of which **72.8 minutes** elapsed before the first event. Peak memory was **10.1 GiB per worker**. The estimate includes one startup per worker and assumes balanced jobs with similar throughput under concurrency. Reuse each initialized process across many angular points.

The pilot used zero field and omitted the inner tracker and beam pipe. It sampled one azimuth. The Geant4 gun rounded the input momenta to six significant figures, giving a maximum \(p_T\) offset of **57 keV** from 50 GeV. [Timing report and reproduction recipe]([redacted]

The repository requires a draft PR. Automatic approval review blocked publication because it would send the local benchmark and session records to GitHub. May I publish the report, recipe, and required project and session records to `asalzburger/nodd`?
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: so, In total you have 10 000 electrons produced now ?
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: The new pilot produced **100 electrons total**, split into four groups of 25. The **110,000 events** were the proposed full scan used for the compute estimate.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: How can a single electron take 10 s but 100 events take 78 mins ?
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text:
**About 73 of the 79 minutes were startup.** DDG4 spent about 66 minutes building the lookup for 531,936 sensitive volume paths, then Geant4 spent another 6½ minutes preparing the first run.

The **100 electrons themselves took about 6 minutes**, averaging **3.6 seconds per electron**. The slowest group, at 503 GeV, took **8.3 seconds per electron**.

Each DDSim worker pays the startup cost once and can then process many angular points in the same session.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: I see ... we will have to investigate the DDG4 startup time
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: I’ll trace the 66-minute DDG4 lookup build using the saved process profile and the source for the installed version. I’ll check which part of startup scales with the detector geometry.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text:
I traced the **66-minute DDG4 startup bottleneck** to assembly placement lookup. For each sensitive path, DDG4 scans the outer assembly’s placement list until it finds the matching path. The barrel alone puts about **8.8 million placements** in one list. The saved CPU profile lands on the path comparison inside that loop. [DDG4 placement registration](https://github.com/AIDASoft/DD4hep/blob/v01-38/DDG4/src/Geant4AssemblyVolume.cpp#L80-L97) · [Lookup loop](https://github.com/AIDASoft/DD4hep/blob/v01-38/DDG4/src/Geant4VolumeManager.cpp#L229-L243)

| Sectors | Sensitive paths | Lookup build time |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 33,246 | 19.4 s |
| 2 | 66,492 | 52.2 s |
| 4 | 132,984 | 195.1 s |
| 16 | 531,936 | 65.9 min |

Doubling from two to four sectors increased lookup time **3.7×**. I stopped a separate template-splitting test once source inspection showed that the lookup still groups placements under the same outer assembly. [Local measurements]([redacted]

The fix I’d test is **indexing the assembly placements by their full path**. The acceptance check would be identical cell IDs for all 531,936 sensitive paths, followed by a fresh startup timing.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: Is there a way this can be done better in the DD4hep geometry?
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: I’ll check where the current Si–W geometry can use real DD4hep mother volumes to preserve the Geant4 hierarchy and avoid the large assembly lookup.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text:
Yes. I’d make each repeated Si–W wedge a **real DD4hep `Volume` with a solid and material**. Build one logical barrel wedge and place it 16 times. Build one logical endcap wedge and place it 16 times per side using the existing transforms. Geant4 can then reuse the daughter geometry across sectors. The current nested `Assembly` objects flatten those daughters into millions of placements. [DD4hep manual on volumes and assemblies]([external URL redacted; see source journal])

The outer assembly can stay as a grouping node for the wedge envelopes. I’d keep the existing layer and board construction inside each wedge for the first test. That makes the change small enough to measure how much startup improves from preserving the sector hierarchy alone. [Barrel factory]([redacted] · [Endcap factory]([redacted]

I’d prototype the **barrel first**. Fill the envelope with the exact material it displaces, preserve the physical cracks and sensor transforms, and verify overlaps, material rays, and the decoded IDs of all **359,904 barrel sensors**. Then time the same zero-event startup. The speedup is still unmeasured.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: Can you try a Prototype? Don’t change the baseline yet.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: I’ll use the acts-spack workflow to verify the runtime, then build a barrel prototype in an ignored test directory. I’ll compare its startup and sensor IDs against the stock geometry using the same sector count.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text:
The isolated Si–W barrel prototype worked. Reusing one real DD4hep wedge volume cut **DDG4 map construction from 175.4 s to 1.09 s**, about **161× faster** in the matched four-sector test. The prototype lives in an ignored build directory, and the baseline checkout is clean.

| Barrel geometry | Sensitive paths | DDG4 map build | Total zero-event startup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Stock, 4 sectors | 89,976 | 175.4 s | 182.6 s |
| Prototype, 4 sectors | 89,976 | 1.09 s | 6.57 s |
| Prototype, 16 sectors | 359,904 | 4.21 s | 10.86 s |

All matched sensors kept their **IDs, materials, positions and orientations**. The full prototype resolved all **359,904 expected sensor IDs**, and 81 material rays agreed with the stock geometry. A zero-field electron at \(p_T=50\) GeV also transported successfully and saved 874 valid barrel hit cells.

These measurements cover the isolated barrel. Endcap adaptation, full-detector overlap checks and shower-response validation remain follow-up work. [Measured results]([redacted] · [Reproduction recipe]([redacted]
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: Ok, repeat that for the Endcap.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: I’ll repeat the prototype test for both Si–W endcaps in an isolated build directory. I’ll use the acts-spack workflow to verify the runtime, then check startup, sensor IDs, material paths, and electron transport on each side.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text:
The isolated Si–W endcap prototype cut **DDG4 map construction from 32.9 s to 4.58 s**, a **7.2× speedup** in the matched test with four wedges per side. The baseline checkout is clean.

| Endcap geometry | Sensor paths | DDG4 map build | Total zero-event startup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Stock, 4 wedges per side | 43,008 | 32.9 s | 37.1 s |
| Prototype, 4 wedges per side | 43,008 | 4.58 s | 7.91 s |
| Prototype, 16 wedges per side | 172,032 | 17.82 s | 21.68 s |

The full endcap prototype resolved all **172,032 expected sensor IDs**, and 144 material rays agreed with stock. Both zero-field electron smoke tests at \(\eta=\pm2\) passed. The initial readback flagged three deposits in the opposite endcap from the negative-side shot. Their saved positions matched the sensor planes encoded in their IDs.

With **both barrel and endcap prototypes** in the same ECAL-only compact, DDG4 mapped all **531,936 sensor paths in 23.5 s**, versus **65.9 minutes** in the stock pilot. Total zero-event startup was **31.5 s**. [Measured results]([redacted] · [Reproduction recipe]([redacted]
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: Ok change the default implementation to the new, faster description and make a PR.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text: I’ll put the faster Si–W wedge hierarchy on a dedicated branch, then check the maintained exporter, sensor IDs, material paths, and transport before opening a draft PR. I’ll verify the Spack runtime again for the native checks.
events.content_kind: visible_message; conservative redactions recorded in source

events.text:
Opened [draft PR #129](https://github.com/asalzburger/nodd/pull/129). It makes reusable wedge volumes the **LAYOUT-001 default** for the Si–W barrel and both endcaps. Standalone exports retain the legacy format for existing fixtures.

The ECAL-only DDG4 map build fell from **65.9 minutes to 23.0 seconds**. All **531,936 sensor IDs and transforms** and **65 material rays** agreed with stock. The full tracker-plus-ECAL scan found **zero overlaps at 10 nm**, and three electron transport smoke tests passed.
